hints: Start from the titre values to find moles of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ in $15.20\text{ cm}^3$ using $n = c \times V$ with volume in $\text{dm}^3$.
Use the balanced equation $2\text{MnO}_4^-$ to $5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\text{H}_2$ to convert to moles of acid in the $25.0\text{ cm}^3$ aliquot, then scale up by $100/25 = 4$ for the whole extract.
Convert total moles to mass with $M_r = 90$ for $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\text{H}_2$, then express as a percentage of the $40.0\text{ g}$ spinach sample.
walkthrough:
Find moles of manganate(VII) actually used**
Picture the burette delivering purple solution until the colour just persists. Moles is concentration times volume in $\text{dm}^3$:
$$n(\text{MnO}_4^-) = 0.0200 \times \frac{15.20}{1000} = 3.04 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$
This is your starting amount, keep all figures for now.

Convert to moles of ethanedioic acid with the 2 to 5 ratio**
Look at the equation: $2\text{MnO}_4^- + 6\text{H}^+ + 5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 10\text{CO}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Two moles of oxidant react with five moles of acid, so multiply by $5/2$:
$$n(\text{acid in 25.0 cm}^3) = 3.04 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{5}{2} = 7.60 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$
Remember this is only the $25.0\text{ cm}^3$ portion titrated. The original filtrate was made up to $100\text{ cm}^3$, so multiply by 4:
$$n(\text{total}) = 7.60 \times 10^{-4} \times 4 = 3.04 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Turn total moles into percentage by mass**
$M_r(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\text{H}_2) = (2 \times 12) + (4 \times 16) + 2 = 90$. Mass in the whole $100\text{ cm}^3$, which came from $40.0\text{ g}$ spinach, is:
$$m = 3.04 \times 10^{-3} \times 90 = 0.2736\text{ g}$$
$$\% = \frac{0.2736}{40.0} \times 100 = 0.684\%$$
About $0.68\%$ to $0.69\%$. A common slip is forgetting the factor of 4.

hints: Recall which reagents replace the $\text{-OH}$ of a $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group by $\text{-Cl}$ without hydrolysing the product.
walkthrough:
Spot the functional group change**
You are going from $\text{HO}_2\text{C-CO}_2\text{H}$ to $\text{ClOC-COCl}$. Each $\text{-OH}$ on a carbonyl carbon is swapped for $\text{-Cl}$. That is the classic carboxylic acid to acyl chloride conversion, which needs an anhydrous chlorinating agent. $\text{SOCl}_2$ (thionyl chloride) is ideal, $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$ also work.

hints: Think what $\text{COCl}$ gives with excess $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ and with a primary amine, HCl is lost in each case.

Count atoms in $\mathbf{J}$ ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$) and $\mathbf{K}$ ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$) to see if one or two molecules of nucleophile have added, and whether the diamine can link both carbonyls into a ring.
walkthrough:
Build J as a double ester**
Acyl chlorides react vigorously with alcohols to give esters plus $\text{HCl}$. Here both $\text{-COCl}$ groups meet $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, so both become $\text{-COOCH}_3$. That gives $\text{CH}_3\text{O-C(=O)-C(=O)-O-CH}_3$, formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$, exactly matching J.

Build K as a cyclic double amide**
With $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, each $\text{-COCl}$ can form a $\text{-CONH-}$ amide link. Because the diamine has two $\text{-NH}_2$ ends and the acid chloride has two $\text{-COCl}$ ends, one molecule of each can join twice to close a six-membered ring. Draw $\text{O=C-C=O}$ at the top, $\text{NH}$ down each side, and $\text{CH}_2\text{-CH}_2$ across the bottom. That cyclic diamide has formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$.

Final answer: J is dimethyl ethanedioate, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCO-COOCH}_3$.
K is the cyclic diamide (piperazine-2,3-dione): six-membered ring $\text{-CO-CO-NH-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-NH-}$ with two $\text{C=O}$ adjacent and two $\text{NH}$ groups linked by $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$.

hints: Use the Data Booklet $^{13}$C shifts: alkyl $\text{CH}_3$ next to carbon appears near $\delta$ 10 to 20, while carbon attached directly to oxygen is strongly deshielded.
Apply symmetry in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_3$: the two $\text{CH}_3$ carbons are identical to each other, and the two $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$ carbons are identical to each other.
walkthrough:
Assign the solvent peaks by environment**
Ethoxyethane is symmetric: $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_2\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$. There are only two carbon environments. Carbon joined to electronegative oxygen is deshielded to about $\delta$ 60 to 70, while simple alkyl $\text{CH}_3$ stays near $\delta$ 15. So both $\text{CH}_3$ boxes are $\delta$ 15 and both $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$ boxes are $\delta$ 65. The spectrum shows peaks at $\delta$ 15 and $\delta$ 65, those belong to the solvent.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_3$ carbons: $\delta$ 15; $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$ carbons: $\delta$ 65.
So left to right: 15, 65, 65, 15.

hints: Count how many peaks remain after removing the two solvent peaks, and recall what number of peaks tells you about equivalent carbons.
walkthrough:
Read what a single peak means**
After assigning $\delta$ 15 and $\delta$ 65 to ethoxyethane, just one peak is left, near $\delta$ 162 in the carbonyl region, belonging to L. In $^{13}$C NMR each distinct environment gives one signal. One signal for a $\text{C}_4$ molecule means all four carbons are chemically identical, so L must be highly symmetric with no overall dipole, consistent with a cyclic structure.
Final answer: Only one peak remains for L (at $\delta$ ca. 162), so all four carbon atoms in L are in the same environment, equivalent.

hints: Link formulas $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4$, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$ to diacid, mono methyl ester and dimethyl ester of ethanedioic acid.
Match $\delta$ 53 to $\text{OCH}_3$ carbon and $\delta$ 160 to 162 to carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ carbons to predict how many signals each candidate should show.
Use the fact that M is formed by heating N or O with aqueous acid to confirm which compound is the hydrolysis product.
walkthrough:
Translate formulas into esterification level**
L ($\text{C}_4\text{O}_6$) plus $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ gives three products that differ by $\text{CH}_2$ each. That screams stepwise addition of methanol to an anhydride type structure. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4$ must be the parent diacid $\text{HO}_2\text{C-CO}_2\text{H}$ (M), $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$ the dimethyl ester (O, same as J), and $\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$ the half ester $\text{CH}_3\text{OCO-CO}_2\text{H}$ (N).

Check against the carbon-13 data**
$\delta$ 53 is typical for $\text{O-CH}_3$, $\delta$ 160 to 162 is typical for ester or acid $\text{C=O}$. M shows only $\delta$ 162, perfect for two identical acid carbonyls and no methyl. O shows $\delta$ 53 and $\delta$ 160, perfect for two identical methyls and two identical ester carbonyls. N shows all three, $\delta$ 53, 160, 162, because its two carbonyls are different, one ester and one acid.

Confirm with hydrolysis behaviour**
Heating an ester with aqueous acid hydrolyses it to the carboxylic acid. Both N (monoester) and O (diester) give M (diacid) on heating with aqueous acid, exactly as stated. That locks the assignment.

Final answer: M is ethanedioic acid, $\text{HO}_2\text{C-CO}_2\text{H}$ (single $\delta$ 162 peak, both $\text{C=O}$ equivalent).
N is monomethyl ethanedioate, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCO-CO}_2\text{H}$ ($\delta$ 53 for $\text{CH}_3$, $\delta$ 160 and 162 for two non-equivalent $\text{C=O}$).
O is dimethyl ethanedioate, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCO-COOCH}_3$ ($\delta$ 53 for $\text{CH}_3$, $\delta$ 160 for equivalent $\text{C=O}$).

hints: Combine the clues: $\text{C}_4\text{O}_6$, no dipole, one $^{13}$C environment, and ring opening with methanol to give mono and diesters plus diacid.
walkthrough:
Assemble a structure that explains everything**
You need $\text{C}_4\text{O}_6$ with all four carbons equivalent and no dipole. Join two ethanedioyl units head to tail through anhydride $\text{C-O-C}$ links to make a six-membered ring: $\text{O=C-O-C=O}$ on top and the same at the bottom, with the two ring oxygens left and right. Every carbonyl carbon sees the same neighbours, giving one $^{13}$C peak near $\delta$ 162, and the symmetric ring cancels dipoles. Attack by $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ opens the anhydride bonds stepwise to give N, then O, plus M on hydrolysis.
Final answer: L is the cyclic dianhydride (1,4-dioxane-2,3,5,6-tetrone): six-membered ring $\text{-O-CO-CO-O-CO-CO-}$ with four equivalent $\text{C=O}$ carbons.
